**MEMO: Hardware Purchase vs. Utilisation Improvement — Recommendation**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

**Background**

We currently operate a small on-premise cluster of GPU nodes that serves our model inference workloads, internal experimentation, and batch fine-tuning jobs. Over the past quarter, utilisation has been uneven: peak demand on weekday afternoons regularly saturates capacity, while nights and weekends sit largely idle. Queue times during peak hours have grown to the point where engineers are context-switching away while jobs wait, and at least two feature launches were delayed because someone couldn't get a GPU slot when they needed it. The obvious instinct is to buy more hardware. I've looked at the numbers, and I think that instinct is half right at best. My recommendation is that we spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of what we own, with a small, carefully scoped purchase only if specific conditions materialise.

**The case for buying more hardware**

Let me be fair to the purchase option first. Adding capacity is fast to reason about. If we're queueing, more GPUs means shorter queues, full stop. There's no behavioural change required, no new scheduling system to build, no awkward conversations about who gets priority. Latency for interactive work improves immediately and predictably. And our current hardware is aging; buying now, while a particular generation is still available and supported, has some appeal compared to being forced into a purchase later under time pressure.

**The case against buying right now**

The problem is what the purchase costs us beyond the invoice. Capital expenditure on GPUs is large and largely irreversible — the resale market for used accelerators is thin and moves against you quickly, and once the hardware is racked, the money is gone whether we use it well or not. That irreversibility matters more than it first appears, because our demand pattern is itself uncertain. We don't actually know how much of our peak load is genuine need versus poor scheduling. If a third of our peak is jobs that could run overnight, or duplicate experiments that could be consolidated, we'd be buying hardware to solve a discipline problem.

There's also opportunity cost. The budget we'd spend on new nodes is budget we can't spend on the data pipeline work, the observability tooling, or the additional engineer-months that several of us agree would deliver more durable value. And reliability cuts both ways: more hardware means more components, more failure modes, more power and cooling load, and more maintenance surface for a team that is already stretched thin. A larger fleet we can't operate well is worse than a smaller fleet we can.

**What utilisation improvement actually looks like**

The alternative is unglamorous but well understood. We need real scheduling: a queue with priorities, preemption for batch jobs, and guaranteed slots for interactive work, so that a launch-critical experiment doesn't sit behind someone's weekend benchmark. We need to shift genuinely deferrable work — fine-tuning runs, evaluation sweeps, bulk embedding jobs — into off-peak windows, which costs nothing but coordination. We need telemetry good enough to tell us what's actually running, for whom, and whether it justifies its slot; right now we're allocating scarce capacity largely on trust and anecdote. And we need a lightweight policy for reclaiming idle reservations, because our current model of "reserve it and maybe use it" is the single largest source of phantom demand I can identify.

None of this is free. It's probably two to three engineer-weeks of work, plus the ongoing social cost of saying no to each other occasionally. But that cost is an order of magnitude below a hardware purchase, it's reversible — we can adjust policies as we learn — and it produces information we currently lack.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next quarter on utilisation: scheduling, off-peak migration, telemetry, and reservation hygiene. Set a concrete trigger now: if, after that work, peak-hour queue times still exceed a defined threshold — I'd suggest more than thirty minutes for priority jobs on more than two days per week — we proceed with a purchase, scoped to the smallest configuration that closes the gap, with budget pre-approved so we're not re-litigating the decision under pressure.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be honest about what I don't know. Utilisation improvements often deliver less than their advocates promise, because human behaviour is sticky and some peak demand is genuinely inelastic. If our peak is real and irreducible, we'll have spent a quarter learning that, and the purchase case will be stronger and better targeted for it. Conversely, if utilisation work succeeds, we'll have bought ourselves time to purchase deliberately rather than reactively, likely at better prices and with clearer requirements. The asymmetry favours waiting: the downside of trying utilisation first is a quarter of modest friction; the downside of buying first is a large, sunk, possibly unnecessary expenditure.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion decision for the inference cluster

**Background**

We've been running near capacity on our local GPU fleet for about six weeks. Queue times for batch jobs have crept from minutes to hours, and interactive work occasionally waits behind long-running fine-tuning runs. The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in getting more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this trade-off, because the framing matters more than the headline numbers.

**The case for buying**

The straightforward argument for new hardware is that demand is real and growing. Our team's roadmap includes three projects that all assume more compute than we currently have. Buying capacity removes a constraint immediately, and GPUs depreciate whether we use them or not — idle capacity is pure waste. There's also a reliability angle: a second node would give us redundancy we currently lack. Right now, a single hardware failure takes our entire training capability offline, and lead times on repairs for our card generation have been running three to five weeks. That's a genuine operational risk, not a hypothetical one.

**The case for improving utilisation**

But before we spend, we should be honest about what our utilisation actually looks like. Telemetry from the last quarter suggests our fleet sits at roughly 40% average utilisation, with peaks that hit 90%+ and long valleys overnight and on weekends. The problem isn't raw capacity; it's scheduling. Batch jobs grab whole GPUs even when they need a fraction of one. Interactive workloads and training runs collide because we have no priority system. A modest investment in better job scheduling, fractional GPU allocation via MIG, and an overnight queue for non-urgent work could plausibly recover 30–40% more effective capacity from hardware we've already paid for.

The cost comparison is stark. A new node is roughly $85K upfront plus power, cooling, and maintenance — call it $110K over three years. The utilisation work is mostly engineering time: perhaps four to six weeks of one engineer's focus, plus some risk of instability while we tune the scheduler. That's maybe $25K in opportunity cost against the roadmap. Even if the utilisation work only recovers half of what I estimate, it's still several times cheaper per unit of effective capacity.

**Latency and the quality of work**

There's a subtler point, though. Utilisation improvements often trade latency for throughput. If we pack jobs more tightly, interactive work may wait longer behind batch queues unless we build proper preemption — which is the hardest part of the project. Our researchers' iteration speed is arguably our most valuable resource; a scheduler that saves money but adds an hour to every experiment loop could cost more in lost productivity than it saves in hardware. Any utilisation work must protect interactive latency as a first-class constraint, not treat it as an afterthought.

**Reversibility and option value**

This is where I land on sequencing. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible commitment — once purchased, the money is spent, and if demand shifts (a model change, a move to hosted APIs for some workloads), we're stuck with depreciating silicon. Improving utilisation is highly reversible: we can adjust scheduler policies, roll back MIG configurations, and change priorities as we learn. In a period where our workload mix is still evolving, preserving option value has real worth. The utilisation path also teaches us our true demand curve. After three months of better telemetry and scheduling, we'll know precisely what we need — and whether buying is justified at all.

**Recommendation**

I recommend we pursue the utilisation improvements first, with a defined scope and timeline: scheduler upgrade, MIG partitioning for small jobs, and an overnight batch queue, targeted for completion within one quarter. I further recommend we pre-approve the hardware purchase contingent on the outcome — if utilisation work brings our peak headroom above 25% and interactive latency stays flat, we defer the purchase; if not, we buy with the team's full confidence that the constraint is real rather than self-inflicted.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be clear about what I don't know. Our utilisation figures come from coarse telemetry and may understate true contention. Demand forecasts for the next two quarters are soft — two of the three roadmap projects could shrink or shift to external APIs. And scheduler work has a habit of expanding; if we're not at 60% utilisation by end of quarter, that itself is a signal worth taking seriously. The contingency structure protects us against being wrong in either direction.

The worst outcome would be buying hardware to solve a scheduling problem, or spending a quarter optimising when the constraint was real all along. The plan above makes both mistakes cheap to detect and correct.

Happy

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing fleet before committing to any new hardware purchases. We are not saying we will never need more GPUs; we are saying that the evidence we have today does not justify the spend, and that a focused effort on scheduling, batching, and workload consolidation will either close the gap entirely or give us the data to buy with confidence. This is the reversible option, and reversibility matters more than usual here.

**Where we actually stand**

Our utilisation numbers look worse than they are, but not by much. Across the fleet, headline GPU utilisation sits around 38 percent, which invites the obvious question of why we would buy more of something we use barely a third of. The honest answer is that raw utilisation is a misleading metric: much of that idle time is memory residency for models that take minutes to load, and some of it is headroom we deliberately hold for latency-sensitive inference paths. When we adjust for those factors, effective utilisation is closer to 55 to 60 percent. That is still not good, but it means the realistic upside from better utilisation is meaningful rather than transformative — perhaps 20 to 25 percent more effective capacity, not the doubling that the raw numbers suggest.

That estimate carries real uncertainty. Our telemetry on memory residency is patchy, and we have never run a sustained experiment with aggressive model swapping or multi-tenant batching on the inference tier. The 20 to 25 percent figure is an informed guess, not a measured result. This is precisely why we should run the experiment: the cost of finding out is a quarter of engineering time, while the cost of guessing wrong in either direction is much larger.

**The cost picture**

The purchase option on the table is roughly $180K in capital plus a meaningful increase in colocation power and cooling, which we estimate at $3.5K per month recurring. Against that, the utilisation effort is roughly 1.5 engineer-quarters, or about $90K in fully loaded time. On paper the utilisation path is cheaper, but the more important asymmetry is what each option commits us to. Hardware is a bet on our current workload shape persisting. If our inference traffic mix shifts — and it has shifted twice in the last year — sunk accelerators are exactly that: sunk. Engineering time spent on scheduling and batching produces knowledge and tooling that retain value even if the capacity problem comes back, because those systems make any future fleet, purchased or not, cheaper to run.

**Latency and reliability**

The strongest argument for buying is latency. Our p99 inference latency has drifted upward as batch queues have grown, and two of our product teams have flagged it as a user-facing problem. We take this seriously, and we want to be clear that utilisation work is not free of latency risk: tighter packing means less slack, and a poorly tuned scheduler can turn a capacity problem into an outage. This is the genuine trade-off. Our position is that we can improve packing while holding latency SLOs fixed as a hard constraint, and that if we cannot, that failure is itself decisive evidence for buying. Reliability cuts the other way: our current fleet has no single point of failure, and adding a small number of new nodes would actually concentrate risk unless we bought enough to spread across racks — which pushes the purchase toward the larger, harder-to-reverse end of the scale.

**Opportunity cost**

The utilisation effort is not free. It would consume the same two engineers who are currently slated to build the fine-tuning pipeline, which several stakeholders consider our highest-value project this half. Delaying that work has a real cost, and we do not want to bury it. Our proposal is to timebox the utilisation work to one quarter with a pre-agreed decision gate: if effective capacity has not improved by at least 15 percent, or if latency SLOs have been threatened more than twice, we escalate the hardware request immediately with the data in hand.

**What we are asking for**

Approve one quarter of focused utilisation work with a hard decision gate at the end, and pre-approve the hardware purchase contingent on the gate failing. If the experiment succeeds, we defer roughly $180K and likely avoid it altogether. If it fails, we buy with evidence rather than instinct, and we will have a better-run fleet to add the new hardware to. Either way, we end the quarter knowing more than we do today, which is more than can be said for simply ordering more machines and hoping the utilisation question goes away.

We are happy to walk through the numbers in detail at Thursday's planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Status and problem**

Our inference cluster is running hot. Peak-hour GPU utilisation sits around 85–90%, queue times for batch jobs have crept from minutes to nearly an hour, and we have twice had to deprioritise experimental workloads to keep customer-facing latency within SLA. The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware now or invest in squeezing more out of the fleet we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this trade-off and make a recommendation.

**The case for buying**

Buying capacity is simple and fast in its effect. Lead time on new accelerators is currently four to six weeks, and once installed, headroom problems largely disappear for a year or more. It also buys us reliability in a literal sense: a larger fleet means a single failed card or node degrades us less, and we can keep a genuine spare pool rather than running everything at the edge of saturation. Right now, if two nodes go down during a peak window, we breach SLA. That is a real business risk, not a hypothetical one.

**The case against buying — and for utilisation work**

The counterargument is cost, and not just the purchase price. At current utilisation patterns, I estimate roughly 30–35% of our GPU-hours go to idle or poorly packed work: models held resident for sporadic traffic, batch jobs scheduled conservatively, and fragmentation where a job needs 80GB and the only free card has 40GB free. If we recover even half of that, we defer a hardware purchase by two to three quarters, which at our scale is a meaningful capital saving. There is also an opportunity cost in the other direction: every dollar spent on hardware we don't yet need is a dollar not spent on the model-quality and product work that actually differentiates us.

The utilisation work itself is not free, though. Quantisation of our two largest models, dynamic batching, better scheduling, and moving dev/experiment workloads to off-peak windows is realistically six to eight weeks of engineering time from two people — time not spent on the roadmap. And some of it carries risk: aggressive quantisation changes model behaviour, and tighter packing means less slack when something fails. We would be trading reliability margin for cost efficiency, and we should be honest that we're doing so.

**Reversibility**

This is where I think the decision actually turns. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible at our scale. If we buy and demand doesn't materialise, we own depreciating assets and pay power and hosting regardless. If we invest in utilisation and it doesn't fully deliver, we've spent engineering time, but we've also built scheduling and batching infrastructure that pays off permanently — and we can still buy hardware afterwards, having lost perhaps six weeks. The utilisation path is the reversible one, and it preserves our option to buy later with better information about our true demand curve. Buying now, by contrast, forecloses little but commits capital on the assumption that current growth continues, which is exactly the assumption I'm least confident about.

**Recommendation**

Invest in utilisation first, with a defined trigger to buy. Specifically: commit two engineers for eight weeks to quantisation, dynamic batching, and scheduling improvements, targeting a reduction of peak utilisation to below 70%. If we hit that, we defer purchase and reassess in Q3. If we miss it — or if demand growth pushes us back above 85% before the work lands — we proceed with the hardware order immediately, having lost only weeks, not quarters. I'd also propose we pre-qualify a vendor and pricing now so that, if the trigger fires, procurement doesn't add another month of lead time.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag what I don't know. Our demand forecast has been wrong in both directions this year; a large customer win could make this whole analysis moot within weeks. Quantisation gains are model-dependent, and our largest model may resist the 30% recovery I'm assuming. And there's a hidden variable in reliability: our current failure rate data covers only twelve months, which may understate tail risk. If the team believes the reliability exposure is worse than I've described, I'd weight the purchase case more heavily.

My overall confidence in the recommendation is moderate — roughly 65/35. The asymmetry of reversibility is what tips it, not certainty about the numbers. I'm happy to walk through the utilisation data in detail at Thursday's review.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide between two paths: purchasing additional local GPU hardware, or investing engineering time to raise utilisation on the machines we already own. After several weeks of measurement and discussion, we recommend the second option — improving utilisation first — with a small, pre-approved budget held in reserve for hardware if our assumptions prove wrong. Here is the reasoning.

The case for buying more hardware is easy to state. Our p99 latency on the primary inference cluster has crept above the 400ms threshold that the product team considers acceptable during peak hours, and the obvious fix for saturation is more capacity. But the obvious fix is not always the right one. When we instrumented the fleet properly, we found that average GPU utilisation sits around 38%, with individual nodes ranging from 12% to 70%. The problem is not that we lack compute; it is that our compute is badly distributed. Batch sizes are conservative, models are pinned to specific nodes rather than scheduled dynamically, and overnight traffic troughs leave expensive silicon idle for six to eight hours a day. Buying more hardware in this state would mean paying to replicate our inefficiency.

The cost asymmetry matters here. A modest expansion of the cluster would run to roughly $180K in capital plus increased colocation and power, and that spend is largely irreversible. GPUs depreciate quickly, our vendor lock-in on the current interconnect makes resale awkward, and once the machines are racked, the operating expense continues whether or not we need them. Improving utilisation, by contrast, costs perhaps six weeks of two engineers' time — call it $60K fully loaded — and the work is inherently valuable regardless of outcome. Better batching, dynamic scheduling, and model consolidation onto shared serving infrastructure are improvements we would want even if we later bought hardware anyway. That reversibility is worth a great deal: if utilisation work stalls or delivers less than projected, we have lost time but gained knowledge, and the hardware option remains fully open.

Latency deserves honest treatment, because it is the strongest argument on the other side. Some of our latency tail is genuinely caused by queueing at peak, and no amount of scheduling cleverness fully eliminates queueing when demand exceeds capacity for sustained periods. Our modelling suggests utilisation work can cut p99 by 25–35% at peak, which likely brings us back under threshold most days — but "most days" is doing real work in that sentence. If the product roadmap adds a latency-sensitive feature in Q3, as has been floated, the margin we recover may be thinner than we'd like. This is the principal uncertainty in our recommendation, and it is why we propose holding the hardware budget as a pre-approved contingency rather than abandoning it. Deciding now to defer purchase is not the same as deciding never to purchase.

Reliability cuts both ways. More nodes means more redundancy, which is a genuine reliability gain. But our incident history tells a more nuanced story: the two worst outages last quarter were caused by configuration drift across an over-provisioned, under-monitored fleet, not by capacity exhaustion. A smaller, better-utilised, more carefully orchestrated fleet is in some ways easier to keep healthy than a larger, sprawling one. Consolidation does concentrate risk, though — a single well-used node going down takes more work with it — so the utilisation plan must include better failover and health-checking, which we've scoped into the effort.

There is also the opportunity cost of the alternative. Those same engineers, if assigned to a hardware procurement and migration, would spend their quarter on racking, networking, and re-benchmarking rather than on the serving-layer improvements that the platform roadmap has needed for a year. Buying hardware consumes the very capacity we'd need to make the new hardware useful.

So the recommendation: fund the utilisation programme now, set a hard review point eight weeks out with concrete success criteria (p99 under 400ms at the 95th-percentile peak day, fleet utilisation above 55%), and pre-approve the hardware purchase to execute immediately if we miss. This sequencing costs us at most a quarter of delay in the worst case, and in the likely case it saves us a substantial, irreversible spend on capacity we may not need. We think the expected value clearly favours patience, and we're prepared to be held to the numbers.

Happy to walk through the measurement data with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Local AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've reached the point where our local GPU fleet is running hot. Queue times for inference jobs have crept up, training runs are getting scheduled around each other, and a few engineers have started quietly routing work to cloud APIs to avoid waiting. That last detail deserves attention: when people route around internal infrastructure, it's a signal that the perceived cost of using what we own has exceeded the perceived cost of alternatives. The question in front of us is whether to buy more hardware or to invest in squeezing more out of the fleet we already have. My recommendation is that we do the latter first, deliberately and with a deadline, before committing capital to new machines.

The case for buying is straightforward and not wrong. Hardware prices are what they are, our workload forecast shows growth, and adding capacity is the fastest way to make the queue-time problem disappear. But that speed is exactly what should make us suspicious. Buying more capacity is the expensive version of fixing a scheduling problem, and we haven't yet demonstrated that our problem is a capacity problem rather than a utilisation problem. Current telemetry suggests our fleet sits at roughly 40–55% utilisation depending on the day, with long idle stretches overnight and sharp contention during working hours. That profile is characteristic of poor bin-packing and manual scheduling, not of a fleet that is genuinely too small. If we buy now, we will spend real money to formalise an inefficient pattern, and the new hardware will inherit the same scheduling habits that produced the current bottleneck.

The utilisation path, by contrast, is cheap in cash terms but expensive in attention. It means building a proper job queue with priorities, enabling batch size tuning and model quantisation where quality tradeoffs are acceptable, consolidating inference endpoints so small models share accelerators, and possibly moving batch training workloads to overnight windows. None of this is glamorous, and it will consume perhaps three to four engineer-weeks that would otherwise go to product work. That opportunity cost is real and I don't want to minimise it. But it is bounded, reversible in the sense that the tooling we build retains value regardless of what we later buy, and it produces information. If after this work utilisation stabilises at 75% or higher and queues still hurt, we will know with confidence that we need capacity — and we'll buy it with a much better sense of how much and what kind.

Latency considerations cut both ways and deserve honest treatment. Local hardware, well-utilised, gives us predictable tail latency for interactive inference and freedom from cloud pricing volatility and rate limits. But a congested local fleet has worse tail latency than a cloud API, because our queueing is worse than theirs. Improving utilisation directly attacks the queueing term, which is where most of our latency pain lives today. Reliability is a related argument for the utilisation path: a fleet with headroom absorbs failures gracefully, and better scheduling with explicit priorities means that when something does fail, the important work still runs. Buying more hardware without improving operations just means we have more machines that can fail in less interesting ways.

There is also a reversibility asymmetry worth naming. Capital hardware is a one-way door in practice — it depreciates, it consumes rack space and power, and once purchased it shapes our architecture around its existence. Scheduling and consolidation work is a soft door: if we later buy hardware, the tooling still helps; if we don't, we've lost nothing but time. When two options have similar expected value, the reversible one should win, and here the reversible option also happens to be the cheaper one up front.

I want to acknowledge the genuine uncertainty in this recommendation. Our workload forecast could be wrong in either direction. If a new product initiative lands next quarter and inference demand doubles, the utilisation work will have bought us time but not capacity, and we'll be buying hardware under time pressure, which is when bad purchasing decisions happen. Conversely, if demand flattens, new hardware would have been a costly mistake. The utilisation path hedges both scenarios better than the purchase path does, which is a large part of why I favour it.

Concretely: I propose we spend the next six weeks on the scheduling, batching, and consolidation work, with a clear success criterion — interactive queue times under two minutes at 70%+ fleet utilisation. If we hit that bar and demand keeps growing, we bring a hardware purchase proposal to leadership with real data behind it. If we miss it, we'll have learned something important about where the bottleneck actually lives.

Happy to walk through the utilisation telemetry with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Recommendation on our next capacity decision

We've reached the point where our inference and fine-tuning workloads are bumping against the ceiling of the eight GPUs we currently own. The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase another node or invest the next quarter in squeezing more out of what we already have. After looking at the numbers and, more importantly, at how our utilization actually behaves week to week, I'm recommending we spend the next quarter improving utilization before we buy anything. Here's the reasoning, along with where I think it could be wrong.

The case for buying is straightforward and not stupid. Our p95 batch latency has degraded from 340ms to 610ms over the past two months, and we've had to queue or shed low-priority jobs during the two peak windows each day. Every quarter we wait, we're presumably paying some cost in degraded product experience and in engineering time spent working around constraints. Hardware lead times are also nontrivial, so if we do eventually buy, starting the procurement conversation early has value in itself.

But when we actually instrumented the fleet, the picture changed. Our headline utilization number looks respectable at around 70 percent, but that average hides a lot. Roughly a third of our capacity is consumed by batch jobs — embedding refreshes, evaluation runs, fine-tuning experiments — that are scheduled whenever someone remembers to run them, not when the hardware is free. Meanwhile, our interactive inference traffic is bursty and predictable: heavy from 9am to noon and again from 2pm to 6pm, with genuine slack overnight and on weekends. In other words, we don't have a capacity shortage so much as a scheduling shortage. Batch work is colliding with interactive work at the worst possible moments, and idle capacity is sitting there at the times when we could be absorbing it.

That reframes the cost question. A new node is roughly $180K up front plus power, cooling, rack space, and — the number people forget — the ongoing operational burden of managing more hardware: driver updates, failure handling, and the cognitive load of a larger fleet. Improving utilization, by contrast, is mostly an engineering-time investment: a proper job queue with priorities, moving batch work into the overnight window, enabling memory-efficient batching, and possibly splitting one or two monolithic services so they can be scheduled independently. Our estimate is six to eight engineer-weeks. Even with generous assumptions about engineer cost, that's a fraction of the hardware spend, and it produces capabilities — real scheduling, real observability — that we'd need anyway even after buying more hardware.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about that. Better utilization means running the hardware closer to its limits, which leaves less headroom for spikes and failures. If we fill the overnight window with batch jobs, a job that overruns can bleed into the morning peak and cause exactly the latency degradation we're trying to avoid. This is a real risk, but it's a manageable one: hard deadlines on batch jobs, preemption, and a small deliberate reserve of capacity for interactive traffic. Buying hardware, by contrast, does improve reliability in the crude sense that more machines means more slack — but it also means more components that can fail and more surface area to operate.

The strongest argument for the utilization path, though, is reversibility. If we spend a quarter on scheduling and it doesn't deliver enough headroom, we've lost some engineer-time and we still have the option to buy — likely with better information about what we actually need, which might mean a smaller purchase or a different configuration. If we buy first and the demand we were worried about doesn't materialize, that capital is gone. Hardware is a one-way door with a maintenance contract attached; scheduling improvements are a door we can walk back through. There's also an opportunity cost to buying now: the hardware market is moving quickly, and a purchase deferred two quarters is likely to get us more performance per dollar.

Where could this recommendation be wrong? If our traffic grows faster than the 15 percent monthly we're currently projecting, utilization work becomes a treadmill we can't win, and we'd be better off buying immediately and doing both in parallel. If a major customer commitment lands next quarter, the calculus shifts too. My suggestion: commit to the utilization work now, define a concrete trigger — sustained p95 latency above 500ms after scheduling improvements, or utilization above 85 percent for two consecutive weeks — that automatically opens the procurement conversation. That way we're not choosing between the options so much as sequencing them sensibly.

I'd like agreement on this direction by end of week so we can staff the scheduling work properly.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference fleet

We've reached the point where our local GPU fleet is running hot. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and the natural instinct is to open a purchase order. Before we do, I want to lay out the case as I see it, because I think the right answer is more nuanced than "buy more" or "squeeze harder," and I want us to decide deliberately rather than by default.

**The case for buying**

The honest argument for new hardware is that our peak demand is real, growing, and increasingly latency-sensitive. The product team's roadmap — the interactive assistant features shipping next quarter — assumes response times we currently cannot deliver at the 95th percentile. Hardware solves that immediately and completely. It also buys insurance: if a node fails during an incident, we have headroom to absorb the loss without degrading user experience. There's a real reliability argument here that utilisation work cannot fully address. You cannot schedule your way out of a dead GPU.

**The case against buying, for now**

But the numbers give me pause. Our fleet-level utilisation sits around 40%, which is poor by any industry standard. The problem isn't capacity; it's that capacity and demand live in different hours. Our batch jobs run overnight on the same cards that sit idle each morning, while the interactive workload peaks midday on cards that then starve the batch queue. We are, in effect, buying peak capacity twice and using neither well. A new purchase made before we fix this would lock in the dysfunction at roughly double the necessary cost.

There's also the opportunity cost to weigh. The capital for two additional high-end nodes is roughly equivalent to a full engineering hire for a year, and the person we'd most want to hire is exactly the one who could build the scheduling and batching improvements that might make the purchase unnecessary. Spending the money on metal forecloses spending it on people, and people compound; metal depreciates.

**Reversibility matters**

This is the point I keep returning to. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible decision — once purchased, the money is spent, and we're committed to the power, cooling, and maintenance overhead whether or not demand materialises. Improving utilisation is reversible and iterative: if a scheduling change makes latency worse, we roll it back in an afternoon. When one option is reversible and the other is not, and both plausibly address the problem, the reversible option should be tried first unless the cost of being wrong is severe. I don't believe it is. If we spend six weeks on utilisation work and it only gets us halfway, we've lost six weeks and gained real information about our true capacity needs.

**What I propose**

Run a focused, time-boxed utilisation effort over the next six weeks. The highest-value moves are consolidating the fragmented small jobs that currently pin whole GPUs for trivial workloads, shifting batch processing fully into the overnight window with a hard cutoff, and enabling dynamic batching on the inference services, which our own benchmarks suggest could absorb a substantial share of peak load on its own. In parallel, we instrument properly: per-workload latency percentiles, queue depth, and true utilisation per card, so that any future purchase decision rests on evidence rather than anecdote.

If, at the end of that period, the 95th-percentile latency for interactive work still misses our target during business hours, I will sponsor the hardware purchase without further debate — and we'll do it with a much sharper understanding of exactly how many nodes we need, which may well be fewer than we'd buy today.

**Uncertainty I want to acknowledge**

I could be wrong about the ceiling of utilisation gains. Some of our latency problems may be inherent to model size and batch interaction, not scheduling, and no amount of clever orchestration fixes physics. There's also execution risk: the six-week effort depends on engineers who have product commitments, and slipping timelines could leave us worse off than if we'd simply bought capacity. Finally, demand forecasts are forecasts; if the next quarter's traffic doubles, the whole calculus shifts toward hardware regardless of how well we schedule.

My recommendation, then: improve first, buy second, and set the decision date now so this doesn't drift. I'd like to align on this in Thursday's planning session.

**Internal Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI hardware — expansion vs. utilisation
**Date:** [Date]

We've been running our local inference and training workloads on a small pool of GPUs for about a year now, and we've hit the point where the queue is no longer abstract. Jobs wait. Experiments get batched into overnight runs. People quietly schedule around the hardware instead of the hardware serving them. The question on the table is whether we buy more cards or invest the next quarter in squeezing more out of what we own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the right answer is less obvious than it looks, and I'd like us to decide it together rather than by default.

The case for buying is the easy one to make. Our utilisation numbers look healthy on paper — the cards are busy most of the day — but "busy" is not the same as "useful." A meaningful fraction of our GPU-hours go to jobs that are small, poorly batched, or run at low efficiency because someone needed a result now and grabbed whatever was free. From a pure throughput standpoint, we could plausibly recover twenty to thirty percent of capacity with better scheduling, batching, and a shared job queue that stops the loudest voice from winning. That's a real number, and it's essentially free compared to the capital cost of new hardware.

But throughput isn't the whole story, and this is where I want to push back on the pure-utilisation position. Latency matters, and it matters in a way that utilisation graphs hide. When a researcher has to wait four hours to iterate on an idea, the cost isn't the GPU time — it's the idea they didn't have, the experiment they didn't run, the bug they found a week later than they would have. Our team's output is limited by iteration speed more than by raw compute. Squeezing utilisation up usually means squeezing latency up too: fuller queues, longer waits, more batching. There's a real tension there, and I don't think we can optimise both simultaneously. If we push utilisation to ninety percent, wait times will get worse before they get better, and morale along with them.

Then there's reliability, which we've been lucky on so far and shouldn't count on continuing to be. Right now, one card going down takes a noticeable bite out of capacity, and two going down at once would be genuinely painful. More hardware is also redundancy. That argument is weaker than it sounds — a second card of the same model shares failure modes with the first — but it's not nothing, and it's worth weighing against the fact that our current setup has no meaningful headroom for a hardware incident.

On cost: new hardware is a capital expense with a depreciation clock ticking on it. GPU prices are volatile, and anything we buy now is likely to look mediocre in eighteen months as the market moves. That's an argument for buying less, later, and only when we're sure the demand is durable. It's also an argument for the utilisation path, which costs engineering time — real, scarce engineering time — rather than cash. And that's the opportunity cost I keep coming back to: the engineers who would do the scheduling and batching work are the same people who'd be shipping product features. A quarter of infrastructure polish is a quarter of product we don't build. Buying hardware, by contrast, is mostly a procurement decision that costs money rather than attention.

Which brings me to reversibility, the factor I think should tip this. Money spent on hardware is hard to un-spend; cards depreciate, and reselling them is a hassle at a loss. Engineering effort on scheduling and batching is largely recoverable — the tooling we build (a proper job queue, better monitoring, model quantisation where it makes sense) has value even if we later buy hardware anyway. The utilisation path is the reversible option. The purchase is the committed one.

**My recommendation:** spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation — a shared scheduler, aggressive batching, quantisation for inference workloads, and honest instrumentation so we can see where hours actually go — and set a concrete trigger now: if, after that work, p95 job wait times still exceed two hours during working hours, we approve the hardware purchase without re-litigating the whole question. That gives us a decision framework rather than a one-time judgement call.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My twenty-to-thirty-percent recovery figure is an estimate, not a measurement; if instrumentation shows we can only recover ten, the calculus shifts toward buying sooner. And if the team grows this quarter, all of this changes. The point of the utilisation-first approach isn't that it's certainly sufficient — it's that it buys us information cheaply before we commit capital irreversibly.

Happy to argue
